title: Holiday flight canceled in summer 2026? Your refund and compensation rights
summary: Flight canceled this summer? Know your EC 261 passenger rights to a full refund, rebooking, and up to €600 in cash compensation. Learn more!
body_markdown:
It's 6am at Faro airport, and Mike’s family have already been up for two hours. Suitcases packed, kids buzzing at the promise of home, their own beds, their own duvets. Then the departure board flips: canceled. No explanation, just a short message from the airline asking them to rebook through the app. 200 other passengers are staring at the same screen, and a queue is already forming at the desk.


If a scene like that has happened to you this summer, or you're worried it might happen before your trip is over, here's the good news: a canceled flight isn't just an inconvenience you have to absorb. Depending on why it happened, you could be owed a refund, a replacement flight, and cash compensation of up to €600 per person.


At a glance


#### What you're owed


**Always:** a full refund, or a replacement flight to your destination — your choice, not the airline's.


**Often:** cash compensation of up to €600 per passenger, if the cancellation was the airline's fault and you were told less than 14 days before departure.


**Usually:** care while you wait — meals, drinks, and a hotel if you're stuck overnight.


**Rarely:** nothing beyond a refund, if the cause was a genuine “extraordinary circumstance,” like severe weather or an air traffic control strike.


## When does this apply — and when doesn't it?


Your right to compensation comes from EU passenger rights law, better known as EC 261, and it kicks in when three things line up: your flight departed from an EU airport, or arrived in the EU on an EU airline; the airline told you about the cancellation less than 14 days before departure; and the disruption was within the airline's control — a crew shortage, a technical fault, an IT outage, overbooking.


It doesn't apply, in most cases, when the airline can point to something genuinely outside its control: a storm grounding flights across a region, a wildcat strike by air traffic controllers, or an airport-wide security incident. In those cases you're still entitled to a refund or rerouting, and to be looked after while you wait, but not to the fixed cash payment.


A reform of EC 261 was agreed by EU lawmakers in mid-2026, but it hasn't changed these compensation bands —[read more in our EC 261 reform 2026 explainer](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/what-ec261-reform-means-for-you/) — and it comes with a tighter window to file: you now have 9 months from your flight date to make a claim, so it's worth acting sooner rather than later.


### Two families, two very different summers


Take two families who each had their homebound flight canceled the same week in July. The first was told, the night before departure, that their airline had grounded the aircraft type over a technical fault discovered across the fleet — a decision entirely within the airline's control. They got rebooked the next morning, and compensation on top, because the airline was responsible for the disruption.


The second family's flight was canceled because a regional air traffic control strike shut down half the airspace they were due to fly through. They got the same refund-or-rerouting choice, and the airline covered their unplanned hotel night, but no cash compensation followed, because the strike wasn't something their airline could have prevented. Same disruption on paper, very different outcome — which is exactly why it's worth checking your own case rather than assuming either way.


## What to do, step by step


-


Get the cancellation in writing. A screenshot of the app notification or the email is enough for now.


-


Choose a refund or rerouting yourself. This is your decision, not the airline's — don't let a gate agent assume you want a voucher.


-


Ask for care if you're stuck. Meals, drinks, and a hotel for an overnight wait aren't a favor; they're your right.


-


Be cautious with “goodwill” vouchers. If one's offered instead of cash compensation, ask directly whether you're still entitled to compensation — accepting a voucher shouldn't mean signing away a separate legal right.


-


Keep every receipt if you pay for something yourself, in case you need to claim it back later.


-


Submit your claim. Go straight to the airline, or run a free check in[the AirHelp app](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/app/) , which pulls in your flight details and tells you in minutes whether a claim looks likely to succeed.


## How to claim


The quickest way to find out where you stand is a free eligibility check in[the AirHelp app](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/app/) , which also tracks your flights and flags a claim the moment one looks worth making. If you'd rather see every clause of the regulation first, our[flight cancellation compensation guide](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/flight-cancellation-compensation/) has the full legal detail — this post is deliberately the shorter, practical version. For the refund-versus-rerouting choice specifically, our[flight refund vs compensation](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/flight-refund/) breakdown walks through it step by step.


It's also worth knowing that a **package holiday** doesn't change any of this: if your flight was booked as part of a package, you still have exactly the same rights against the airline, on top of anything your tour operator owes you separately.


If you fly often enough that this feels like a recurring risk, it's worth reading how[AirHelp+](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/airhelp-plus/) changes the math, and pairing it with a decent[flight tracker app](https://www.airhelp.com/en-int/blog/the-5-best-flight-tracker-apps-for-stress-free-travel/) so you hear about a disruption before the airline announces it.


## FAQ


#### What's the difference between a refund and compensation?


A refund gives you back what you paid for the flight, or lets you take an alternative one if you'd rather keep traveling. Compensation is a separate, fixed cash payment for the inconvenience, and only applies when the airline was at fault.


#### Can I still claim if my flight was part of a package holiday?


Yes. Your airline rights apply regardless of how you booked, so a package holiday doesn't reduce what you're owed from the airline.


#### What if the airline blames “extraordinary circumstances”?


Ask for the specific reason in writing. Airlines sometimes cite this too broadly, and a vague explanation isn't the same as a valid one.


#### How long do I have to make a claim?


Under the current rules, you have up to 9 months from your flight date, so it's worth acting while the details, and your evidence, are still fresh.
